verdict.rationale: Two lenses (two ways of reading the same evidence) are both defensible from the original words of Scripture, so the combined claim does not resolve cleanly. The underlying substrate (the foundational concepts the claim sits on) is real and well attested: the word for assembly or church (ekklesia, Strong's G1577) occurs in 112 verses across Acts, the Pauline letters, Hebrews, James and Revelation as a definable assembly; the verb to lead, used as a noun for leaders (hegeomai, Strong's G2233), clusters in Hebrews 13 as a defined oversight relationship that renders account; 1 Corinthians 5:12 sorts persons by inside (eso) and outside (exo); the word for member or limb (melos, Strong's G3196, 24 verses) makes believers organic members of one body. But no single word names a formal membership roll, register, joining covenant or enrollment process. The closest term, to enroll or enlist (katalego, Strong's G2639, used in the phrase 'let a widow be enrolled'), is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) in 1 Timothy 5:9 attached to a widow support list with age criteria, not a congregational roster. Other supporting words are generic and polysemous (carrying multiple senses), given community force only by context: to add (prostithemi), to judge (krino), and inside (eso) and outside (exo) which are mostly literal spatial terms elsewhere. So the bounded, overseen, disciplinable body is warranted while the specific named institution is an inference, not a command.

scripture.reasoning: The discipline procedure escalates to the assembly or church (ekklesia) as the final earthly tribunal (court of judgment): 'tell it to the assembly' (eipon te ekklesia). The article 'the' plus the local court function presupposes a bounded, identifiable body that can hear a case and act, and a person who disregards it (refuse to heed, parakouo) is then treated as an outsider. This requires a recognizable membership boundary in practice but names no roll, register, or covenant document. The verb 'refuse to heed' (parakouo, Strong's G3878) occurs in only 2 verses in the canon (here and Mark 5:36), so the disciplinary 'refuse to hear' sense rests on a near singular use.

Paul contrasts 'those inside' (tous eso) with 'those outside' (tous exo) as the proper scope of the assembly's judgment: 'for what have I to do with judging those outside' (ti gar moi tous exo krinein). The inside and outside pair marks a definite disciplinary edge. The force is sharpened by distribution: 'inside' (eso, Strong's G2080) occurs in only 9 verses and elsewhere is literal spatial (inside the courtyard, the inner man), and 'outside' (exo, Strong's G1854) occurs in 64 verses overwhelmingly literal (go outside, cast outside). The community boundary sense is therefore a contextual idiom Paul applies here, not a fixed technical membership term, and 'judge' (krino, Strong's G2919, 99 verses) is a general judge verb given in-house force only by context.

The readers must obey and submit to their leaders (hegoumenoi, the noun-used form of hegeomai, Strong's G2233) who keep watch (agrupnousin, from agrupneo, Strong's G0069) over their souls as those who will render an account (logon apodosontes, from apodidomi, Strong's G0591). The substantival (noun-used) form of 'to lead' (hegeomai) for leaders clusters in this very chapter (Hebrews 13:7, 13:17, 13:24) plus Acts 14:12 and 15:22, showing a defined accountable oversight relationship in which named leaders answer for named persons. 'Keep watch' (agrupneo) is rare (4 verses) and 'render or give back' (apodidomi) is common and generic (46 verses, mostly 'repay' or 'give back'), so the account-rendering force is carried by the construction 'render an account' (logon apodidomi), not by a dedicated office vocabulary. The verse commands the relationship and the posture but supplies no term for enrollment or formal covenant.

'You are the body of Christ and members individually' (humeis de este soma Christou kai mele ek merous). The word for 'member' or 'limb' (melos, Strong's G3196) appears in 24 verses, and its body sense is dense in 1 Corinthians 12, Romans 12, and Ephesians 4 to 5, but the word is organic body imagery (limb, part of a body) and is also used literally of bodily members (Matthew 5:29 to 30, Romans 6, James 3 to 4). It never denotes an administrative roster entry. So 'membership' in the New Testament sense that is lexically loaded (carried by the actual vocabulary) is organic incorporation into one body, which neither requires nor names a formal roll.

'Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old' (chera katalegestho me elatton eton hexekonta gegonuia). The verb 'to enroll or enlist' (katalego, Strong's G2639) is the single closest lexeme (word entry) in the canon to a formal register, and it is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible), occurring in this one verse only. It governs a specific widow support list with explicit age criteria (sixty years), not a congregational membership roll for all believers. The one place the canon does name an enrollment, it is a narrow benevolence (financial care) roster, which shows the vocabulary for formal lists existed but was not extended to church membership as such.

Those who 'received' (apodexamenoi, from apodechomai, Strong's G0588) the word were baptized and 'were added' (prosetethesan, from prostithemi, Strong's G4369), and the number is counted at about three thousand 'souls' (psuchai). The passive 'were added' plus an enumerated count shows a countable, additive community. But 'to add' (prostithemi) occurs in 18 verses and is a generic add verb (add years to life, add to faith); only the Acts cluster (2:41, 2:47, 5:14, 11:24) carries the 'join the community' sense, and that by context. Acts 2:42 then has them 'devoting themselves continually' (proskarterountes). This is narrative description of conversion and growth, not a prescriptive command to institute formal membership.

complicating_texts.resolution: The 'added' and 'counted' language proves a countable community but is narrative description of conversion and growth, not a command to enroll. The verb 'to add' (prostithemi) is a generic add verb that carries the 'join the community' sense only in the local Acts cluster, so it supports the existence of a bounded body without lexically (by the words themselves) establishing a formal covenanted membership rite. It cuts toward the boundary substrate (the underlying concept) while leaving the named practice unwarranted.

The verb 'to enroll' (katalego, 'let a widow be enrolled') is the one place the canon uses a formal enrollment verb, and it is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) governing a widow support list with an age threshold, not a membership roll for all believers. It cuts both ways: it shows enrollment vocabulary existed, which a membership advocate can cite by analogy, yet the canon never applies it to congregational membership, which a skeptic reads as decisive silence. Because the single occurrence cannot be triangulated (cross-checked against multiple data points) to a general practice, it is addressed but leaves the dispute open.

Where two or three are gathered 'in my name' (eis to emon onoma), Christ is present in their midst. The minimal threshold of two or three for valid gathered action shows the assembly's authority does not depend on a formal roster or institutional scale, which complicates the claim that formal membership is prudentially (practically) essential rather than the gathered body itself being the operative unit.

The word for 'member' (melos) makes believers members of one body, but the word is organic body imagery, never an administrative roster entry. This complicates the proposition by showing that the only lexicalized (vocabulary-carried) sense of 'membership' in the canon is incorporation into the body of Christ, which neither requires nor names a formal local roll, so the named practice is not what the membership vocabulary actually denotes.

variants.note: A direct query of the lexical store returned zero VariantUnit nodes (textual variation entries) on any anchor verse (Matthew 18:15 to 20, 1 Corinthians 5:12 to 13, Acts 2:41 to 42, Hebrews 13:17), and not_in_ecm_scope (outside the ECM apparatus, the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) is true for these passages. The minor apparatus marks visible in the bundle (the placement of 'me' (moi) in 1 Corinthians 5:12, the 'put out' (exarate) spelling in 1 Corinthians 5:13) do not touch the boundary, oversight, or enrollment vocabulary on which the verdict turns, so the verdict holds across plausible readings.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Matthew 18:17 makes the assembly or church (ekklesia) the terminal court of discipline, 1 Corinthians 5:12 sorts persons into 'inside' (eso) and 'outside' (exo), and Hebrews 13:17 commands submission to leaders (hegoumenoi, from hegeomai) who keep watch over souls and render account. Acts 2:41 shows a countable body that can be added to. Together these lexically (by the actual words) warrant a recognizable, accountable, bounded community with a real edge, which is the strongest form of the affirming reading: you can be added, be inside, submit to known leaders, and be removed.

No lexeme (word entry) names a membership roll, register, joining ceremony beyond baptism, or public covenant rite between believer and assembly. The closest enrollment word, 'to enroll' (katalego), is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) for a widow support list, not church membership. The specific institutional form of a formal, publicly covenanted membership that is prudentially (practically) essential is an inference from boundary language, not a command carried by a verb or noun, so the precise stem claim is lexically underdetermined (not settled by the words themselves).

Stated in its strongest form, the only lexicalized (vocabulary-carried) sense of being a member is 'member' or 'limb' (melos), organic incorporation into the one body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:27, Romans 12:5, Ephesians 4:25). On this reading membership is a real and biblical category, but its content is union in the body effected by the Spirit, which is fully present wherever believers are joined to Christ and to one another, independent of any local administrative roll.

Matthew 18:20 grounds valid gathered authority in 'two or three gathered in my name' (in Christ's name), which in its strongest form says the operative unit is the gathered believers in Christ's presence, not a formal membership structure. On this reading making formal membership prudentially (practically) essential adds a requirement the words do not impose.

hermeneutics.notes: The texts converge on a bounded, overseen, disciplinable body (analogia scripturae, the principle that Scripture interprets Scripture, across gospel, narrative, and epistle). The dispute is about whether that substrate (foundational concept) entails the named practice of formal covenanted membership. Two affirming lenses (bounded assembly, organic body) and one negative lens (minimal gathered body) each have lexical footing, and the canon supplies the substrate without ranking the institutional forms, so the lexis (vocabulary) does not settle the compound stem (the multi-part question).

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Does the New Testament vocabulary for the local assembly establish a defined, bounded membership boundary and an accountable oversight relationship, and if so does it lexically (by the actual words used) prescribe a formal public covenanted enrollment as the means of constituting that boundary?
stem_audit.notes: The original stem (question wording) is preloaded twice. First, 'biblically warranted and prudentially essential' pre-judges both the exegetical (interpretive) and the practical verdict before the vocabulary is read. Second, 'public covenanted commitment between believer and local assembly under elder oversight' names a specific institutional ecclesiology (church-government model) that no single lexeme (word entry) carries. The verdict is derived on the original stem and the answer remains disputed: the boundary and oversight substrate (foundational concept) is warranted but the named formal practice is not lexically commanded. Direct canon queries this pass confirmed the prior reading and did not force a change: the word for assembly or church (ekklesia) is dense and pan-canonical New Testament (spread across the whole New Testament, 112 verses), the word for 'member' or 'limb' (melos) is organic body imagery (24 verses, never a roster), the inside (eso) and outside (exo) terms are mostly literal spatial elsewhere, and the one enrollment verb 'to enroll' (katalego) is a hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) for a widow list.

lay_summary: The claim has two parts and the original words of Scripture treat them differently. The first part, that a local assembly has a real edge with people inside and people outside and with leaders who answer for those souls, is carried by the vocabulary. In Matthew 18:17 the offended believer finally tells it to the assembly or church (ekklesia), and that word for the gathered assembly appears in about 112 verses across the New Testament, so it is a settled, recognizable thing. In 1 Corinthians 5:12 Paul speaks of those inside (eso) and those outside (exo), and in Hebrews 13:17 the readers submit to leaders (hegoumenoi, from hegeomai, 'to lead') who keep watch (agrupneo) over their souls and will give an account (apodidomi). Together these show a bounded, accountable, overseen body. The second part is different. There is no word in any of these texts for a membership roll, a register, a joining ceremony beyond baptism, or a signed covenant between a believer and a congregation. The one enrollment word in the whole New Testament, 'to enroll' (katalego), used of widows in 1 Timothy 5:9, occurs exactly once (a hapax, a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible) and governs a widow support list with an age rule, not a church roster. The supporting words are also slippery: 'added' (prostithemi) in Acts 2:41 is a general verb for adding anything, and 'inside' and 'outside' are normally just spatial words for being in or out of a house, given community meaning only by the surrounding sentence. There is one word that does mean 'member', 'member' or 'limb' (melos) in 1 Corinthians 12:27, but it pictures believers as organic parts of one body, like limbs, never as names on a list. So the picture is genuinely mixed. The boundary and the oversight are written into the words. The specific practice named in the claim, a formal publicly covenanted membership that is essential, is a reasonable inference some draw from the boundary, but no lexeme (word entry) states it, and others read the body language and the 'two or three gathered' in Matthew 18:20 as making the gathered believers themselves the operative unit. Because the substrate (foundational concept) is warranted while the named practice is not lexically commanded, the honest reading is disputed rather than a clean yes or no.
